items.title: 9.13 Resistivity and its dependence upon temperature

source_refs.note: Topic 9.13 with Fig. 9.22, Table 9.2, Examples 9.7 and 9.8 and the side box (PDF 210-212, printed 207-209).

blocks.text: It has been seen experimentally that the resistance R of a wire is directly proportional to its length L and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area A. Mathematically R is proportional to L/A, or R = rho L/A ... (9.32), where rho (rho) is a constant of proportionality known as the resistivity or specific resistance of the material of the wire. Resistance is a characteristic of a particular wire, whereas resistivity is a property of the material of which the wire is made. From Eq. 9.32, rho = RA/L ... (9.33).

blocks.title: Resistivity
blocks.text: The resistivity of a material is the resistance of a metre cube of the material. Its SI unit is the ohm-metre (ohm m).

Conductance is another quantity used to describe the electrical properties of materials; it is the reciprocal of resistance: G = 1/R, where G is the conductance. Similarly the conductivity sigma is the reciprocal of the resistivity: sigma = 1/rho ... (9.34). The SI unit of conductivity is ohm^-1 m^-1, or mho m^-1. Table 9.2 shows that silver and copper are the two best conductors; that is the reason most electric wires are made of copper.

The resistivity of a substance also depends on temperature. The resistance of a conductor is due to collisions between the free electrons and the atoms of the lattice. As the temperature rises, the amplitude of vibration of the lattice atoms increases, and so does the probability of their collision with free electrons; the atoms offer a bigger target, that is, their collision cross-section increases with temperature. This makes the collisions more frequent, and hence the resistance of the conductor increases.

Experimentally, the change in resistance of a metallic conductor with temperature is nearly linear over a considerable range of temperature above and below 0 degrees C (Fig. 9.22, variation of the resistivity of copper with temperature). Over such a range the fractional change in resistance per kelvin is known as the temperature coefficient of resistance: alpha = (Rt - R0)/(R0 t) ... (9.35), where R0 and Rt are the resistances at 0 degrees C and t degrees C. As resistivity depends on temperature, Eq. 9.32 gives Rt = rho_t L/A and R0 = rho_0 L/A ... (9.36); substituting into Eq. 9.35, alpha = (rho_t - rho_0)/(rho_0 t) ... (9.37), where rho_0 and rho_t are the resistivities at 0 degrees C and t degrees C. Some substances, like germanium and silicon, have a resistance that decreases with increasing temperature; they have negative temperature coefficients.

blocks.title: Example 9.7
blocks.text: A current of 0.75 A flows through an iron wire when a 1.5 V battery is connected across its ends. The wire is 5.0 m long with cross-sectional area 2.5 x 10^-7 m^2. Compute the resistivity of iron. Solution: R = V/I = 1.5 V/0.75 A = 2.0 ohm. rho = RA/L = 2.0 ohm x 2.5 x 10^-7 m^2/5.0 m = 1.0 x 10^-7 ohm m.

blocks.title: Example 9.8
blocks.text: A platinum wire has a resistance of 10 ohm at 0 degrees C and 20 ohm at 193 degrees C. Find the temperature coefficient of resistance of platinum. Solution: R0 = 10 ohm, Rt = 20 ohm, t = 466 K - 273 K = 193 K. alpha = (Rt - R0)/(R0 t) = (20 - 10)/(10 x 193) = 1/193 K = 5.18 x 10^-3 K^-1.

Inspectors can easily check the reliability of a concrete bridge made with carbon fibres: the fibres conduct electricity, and if sensors show that the electrical resistance is increasing over time, the fibres are separating because of cracks (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: A wire of resistance 4 ohm is doubled on itself; find the new resistance (MCQ 9.7). A copper wire of resistance R is stretched to double its length; find its new resistance (short question 9.5). Why does the resistance of a conductor rise with temperature (short question 9.6)?
blocks.explanation: Doubling on itself halves L and doubles A, so R = rho L/A falls to one quarter: 1 ohm, option (d). Stretching to twice the length keeps the volume the same, so the area halves; L/A becomes four times larger and the new resistance is 4R. In a hotter metal the lattice atoms vibrate with larger amplitude, so the free electrons collide with them more often and their drift is hindered more.

items: R = rho L/A (9.32); resistivity rho = RA/L (9.33), ohm m, a property of the material; conductance G = 1/R; conductivity sigma = 1/rho (9.34), mho m^-1. Silver and copper conduct best.

Hotter lattice, more collisions, larger R; alpha = (Rt - R0)/(R0 t) (9.35) = (rho_t - rho_0)/(rho_0 t) (9.37); carbon, germanium, silicon have negative alpha. Examples: rho(iron) = 1.0 x 10^-7 ohm m; alpha(platinum) = 5.18 x 10^-3 K^-1.
